title: Draining North Holland's lakes with windmills: the Beemster (1612) and other Dutch polders

facts.text: About 27 percent of the Netherlands lies below sea level.
Without dunes and dikes, more than half of the Netherlands would be under water.
About a fifth of the Netherlands has been reclaimed from the sea, lakes, marshes and swamps.
A polder is a piece of low-lying land surrounded by dikes, in which the water level is controlled through inlets and outlets.
In northern Holland, sea water once entered the land through open inlets; when the inlets were closed, the water left behind became lakes.
To drain such a lake, people built a dike all around it, put up windmills and pumped the water out.
Once drained, the fertile clay land was sold to wealthy townspeople for farming.
The draining of these lakes was paid for by companies of investors; the new polders later received the right to govern their own water affairs.
Between 1546 and 1650, more than seventy lakes were drained in what is now the province of North Holland, from about 20 to over 6,000 hectares in size.
The Beemster, a lake in North Holland, was drained in 1612, creating about 7,100 hectares of land.
Other North Holland lakes drained soon after include the Purmer (1622, 2,760 hectares) and the Schermer (1635, 4,770 hectares).
Most lake draining in the Low Countries took place in the first half of the seventeenth century.
Because the land is sinking and the sea is rising, the ground in the Low Countries drops about ten centimeters every hundred years compared with the sea.
Draining peat land exposes it to air; the peat breaks down and the ground sinks, which in the past called for deeper channels and then windmills to pump the water out.
Today Dutch water levels are controlled by water boards using dikes, locks and pumps, and land sinking can only be slowed to about 3 to 5 millimeters a year.
Local water boards responsible for dikes and drainage have existed in the western Netherlands since the Middle Ages; Rijnland's charter dates from 1255.
The Haarlemmermeer, a lake near Haarlem, grew from about 6,600 to 19,500 hectares between 1530 and 1730 as storms ate away its shores.
The Dutch called a lake that kept swallowing land in this way a water wolf.
Work on draining the Haarlemmermeer began in 1840 with a ring canal, and the 18,500-hectare polder was dry in 1852.
The Haarlemmermeer was emptied by only three steam pumping stations, which still exist, and it was then by far the largest Dutch land reclamation.
Derived: the Haarlemmermeer polder (18,500 hectares) is about two and a half times the size of the Beemster (7,100 hectares), and it was drained 240 years later (1612 to 1852).
